title: How to batch print packing slips for multichannel order fulfillment
body_markdown:
Printing packing slips one order at a time is fine until you're running Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy out of the same warehouse — then it turns into a part-time job. This guide walks through the exact workflow for batch printing packing slips across every channel from one queue, without missing an order or double-printing a return label.


**TL;DR**

- Batch printing packing slips across marketplaces requires one consolidated order queue, not five separate seller dashboards.
- Filter orders by carrier and fulfillment status before you print — mixed batches cause the most picking errors.
- A 50-100 order batch is the sweet spot for most warehouses in 2026 — bigger batches slow down verification.
- SellerChamp pulls Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy orders into one packing slip queue so you print once per shift, not once per channel.


## Why this matters

Every marketplace ships its own packing slip format, its own order export, and its own print trigger. Run five channels manually and you're logging into five dashboards every morning just to print paperwork.

That's before you count the errors. A packer working off the wrong slip format, or a batch that mixes FedEx and USPS orders, turns into a mis-ship — and mis-ships cost more in return shipping and support tickets than the software that would have prevented them. Multichannel order fulfillment breaks down at the packing slip step more often than at the listing or inventory step, because it's the one manual touchpoint left after everything else gets automated.

## What you'll need

- Active seller accounts connected on the channels you fulfill from (Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, Etsy, or others)
- A multichannel order management tool that consolidates orders into one queue — [SellerChamp](https://sellerchamp.com/) does this across all major marketplaces
- A packing slip template per channel, or one universal template if your buyers don't need channel branding
- A thermal or laser printer capable of handling your daily order volume
- 15-20 minutes at the start of each fulfillment shift to run and verify the batch

## The steps

### 1. Consolidate every channel's orders into one queue

Batch printing only works if the orders are sitting in one place first. Pulling Amazon orders from Seller Central, eBay orders from My eBay, and Shopify orders from the admin panel separately defeats the purpose before you've printed a single slip.

Connect each sales channel to a multichannel order management platform so new orders land in one unified queue as they come in, tagged by marketplace. Expect this sync to run near real-time — orders placed in the morning should show up in your queue within minutes, not at the next manual export.

**Common mistake:** relying on end-of-day CSV exports from each marketplace. That delays fulfillment by a full cycle and defeats same-day shipping commitments.

### 2. Filter orders by carrier and fulfillment status before batching

Don't print everything sitting in the queue as one giant batch. Filter first by fulfillment status — new, unfulfilled, and paid — then by carrier or shipping method, so USPS and UPS orders don't end up mixed in the same stack.

This matters because packers grab slips in order, and a batch that jumps between shipping methods forces them to sort packages twice: once by slip, once by carrier pickup. Filtering upfront removes that second sort entirely.

**Expected outcome:** a clean batch where every slip in the stack ships the same way, in the same window.

### 3. Select the batch size for the print run

Most warehouses fulfilling 50-200 orders a day get the best throughput printing in batches of 50 to 100 orders at a time in 2026, rather than one 300-order mega-batch. Smaller batches are easier to verify against pick lists and easier to recover from if a printer jam happens mid-run.

High-volume sellers running 500+ orders daily can push batch size up, but should split by zone or carrier cutoff time so the earliest-scheduled pickups print first.

**Common mistake:** batching the entire day's orders at 9 a.m. and letting afternoon orders sit unprinted until the next run.

### 4. Choose the correct packing slip template per channel

Amazon buyers, eBay buyers, and your own Shopify store customers expect different things on a slip — some require no pricing shown (Amazon FBM in particular), others benefit from a branded template that reinforces your store name.

Set a default template per channel inside your order management tool so the correct format applies automatically, instead of a packer manually swapping templates between orders. Getting this wrong on Amazon specifically can trigger a policy violation if pricing appears where it shouldn't.

**Expected outcome:** every slip in the batch matches its channel's requirements without manual template switching.

### 5. Run the print job and check the page count

Before hitting print, confirm the batch order count matches the expected page count — one slip per order unless an order has multiple line items requiring extra pages. A mismatch here is the fastest way to catch a duplicate or a dropped order before it hits the floor.

Run the job to your thermal or laser printer and let it complete fully before touching the output stack. Interrupting a batch mid-print is the single most common cause of skipped orders in fulfillment centers.

**Common mistake:** pulling slips off the printer tray before the job finishes, which reorders the stack and breaks the sequence packers rely on.

### 6. Verify slips against pick lists in sequence

Match the printed batch to your pick list, in order, before packers start pulling inventory. This is the checkpoint that catches an order that got filtered out incorrectly or a slip that printed twice.

Doing this verification after packing starts means errors get caught after the box is sealed, which costs a re-open and a repack. Doing it before costs 60 seconds per batch.

**Expected outcome:** a 1-to-1 match between printed slips and pick list line items before a single item gets pulled.

### 7. Mark the batch as printed and lock it from re-printing

Once a batch is printed and verified, mark those orders as "printed" in your order management system so they don't accidentally get pulled into the next batch run. Without this step, a slip printed at 9 a.m. can reappear in the 1 p.m. batch and generate a duplicate shipment.

**Common mistake:** skipping the status update and relying on memory to track what's already been printed — this fails the moment two people are running batches on the same shift.

### 8. Reconcile shipped orders against the batch at end of day

Close out the day by comparing shipped order counts against printed batch counts across every channel. Any gap points to either an order that printed but never shipped, or a fulfillment status that never got updated back to the marketplace.

This reconciliation step is what keeps your Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy order statuses accurate — which directly affects account health metrics on marketplaces that track late shipments.

## Troubleshooting

- **Slips print with the wrong pricing or no pricing at all.** Check the template assignment for that channel — a default template got overridden or a new order source wasn't mapped to a template yet.
- **Batch printed 48 slips for a 50-order batch.** Two orders were likely still in "pending payment" status and got excluded automatically — check the order status filter before assuming a printer error.
- **Duplicate slips for the same order.** The order wasn't marked "printed" after the last batch, so it re-entered the queue. Lock printed orders immediately after each run.
- **Printer jams mid-batch and the sequence breaks.** Reprint only the missing order range rather than restarting the full batch — most order management tools let you reprint by order number range.
- **Etsy or eBay orders missing from the queue entirely.** The channel connection likely needs re-authorization — marketplace API tokens expire periodically and silently stop syncing new orders.
- **Packing slip totals don't match the invoice sent to the buyer.** This usually means a manual price override happened after the order synced — re-sync the order before reprinting.

## Tools and resources

- A multichannel order management dashboard that consolidates Amazon, eBay, Walmart, Shopify, and Etsy orders in one queue — [SellerChamp](https://sellerchamp.com/) is built specifically for sellers running fulfillment across five or more channels
- A thermal printer rated for your daily batch volume
- Carrier cutoff schedules for each shipping method you offer, so batches print in time for same-day pickup
- A documented packing slip template per channel, reviewed any time a marketplace updates its seller policies


**Run every channel from one queue**

See how SellerChamp consolidates orders, listings, and inventory across marketplaces.

**[Explore SellerChamp](https://sellerchamp.com/)**


## What to do next

Once batch printing is running smoothly, the next bottleneck is usually inventory sync — packing slips only stay accurate if stock counts across channels update the moment an order prints, otherwise you're one oversold SKU away from a cancellation. Get that sync tight before scaling batch size further in 2026.

## FAQ


**What is the best batch size for printing packing slips across multiple marketplaces?**

Most sellers fulfilling 50-200 orders daily in 2026 get the best results batching 50 to 100 orders at a time. Larger daily volumes should split batches by carrier or shipping zone rather than printing everything in one run.

**How do you batch print packing slips for Amazon, eBay, and Shopify at the same time?**

Consolidate orders from all three channels into one order management queue first, then filter and print as a single batch. Printing directly from each marketplace's separate dashboard defeats the purpose of batching.

**Is it against Amazon policy to show pricing on a packing slip?**

Amazon FBM orders should not display pricing on the packing slip in most cases, since Amazon treats this as a policy issue tied to buyer-seller messaging rules. Set a template without pricing as the default for Amazon orders to avoid the risk.

**How much does multichannel order management software cost in 2026?**

Pricing varies by platform and by how many channels and orders you're running, so check current pricing directly on the vendor's site. Most tools scale cost with order volume or connected channel count.

**What causes duplicate packing slips to print for the same order?**

An order that wasn't marked as "printed" after its first batch run re-enters the queue and prints again in the next batch. Locking orders as printed immediately after each run prevents this.

**Can you batch print packing slips without an order management tool?**

Yes, but it means logging into each marketplace separately and exporting orders manually, which doesn't scale past two or three channels. A consolidated queue is what makes true batch printing possible across five or more channels.

**How often do marketplace order sync connections need to be reauthorized?**

API tokens for channels like Etsy and eBay expire periodically and need reauthorization, though the exact interval depends on the marketplace. If orders stop appearing in your queue, check the channel connection status first.

**What's the difference between a packing slip and a pick list?**

A packing slip goes inside the shipped box and confirms the order contents to the buyer, while a pick list is the internal document a warehouse worker uses to pull inventory. Batch printing typically generates both from the same order data.


## One last thing

The reconciliation step at the end of the day — matching shipped counts against printed batch counts — catches more fulfillment errors than any filter or template setting earlier in the process. Sellers who skip it find out about a missed order when the buyer messages asking where it is, which is a far more expensive way to find the same gap.
